classification.difficultyReason: Select the three-root square-sum identity, obtain its inputs from cubic coefficients, and connect the negative result to the impossibility of three real intercepts.

content.prompt:
Let $x^3-2x^2+3x-1=0$ have roots $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.

(a) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.

(b) Hence, explain why the graph of $y=x^3-2x^2+3x-1$ cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.

answer.short: (a) $-2$. (b) If all three roots were real, the sum of their squares would be non-negative. Since the sum is $-2$, the roots cannot all be real, so the graph cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.
answer.worked:
(a)
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)\\&=2^2-2(3)\\&=-2\end{aligned}$$
(b) A cubic has three roots, counting multiplicity. If all three were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\geq0$. Part a gives $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=-2$, so the roots cannot all be real. Hence the graph cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.
